pages.title: A nearly insoluble solid still exchanges ions

blocks.text: Silver chloride appears insoluble, but a small amount dissolves. In a saturated solution touching solid AgCl, ions leave and return to the crystal continuously. A small equilibrium concentration is different from exactly zero dissolution.
The solubility product K(sp) is the equilibrium constant for dissolution of a sparingly soluble ionic solid into its ions under specified conditions.

pages.transition: Write the dissolution equation before writing its product.

pages.title: Stoichiometry determines the concentration powers

blocks.text: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), so K(sp) = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] in the dilute concentration convention. The pure solid is omitted. For CaF₂(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻, K(sp) = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]².
The coefficient 2 becomes an exponent in K(sp) and a factor in ion concentrations. Missing either use leads to an incorrect solubility.
Molar solubility s is the number of moles of solid that dissolve per litre of saturated solution.

pages.transition: Start with the simplest one-to-one ion stoichiometry.

pages.title: Worked solubility of a one-to-one salt

blocks.text: Teacher-created rounded data: K(sp)(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at the stated temperature. In pure water, [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s. Therefore s² = K(sp), giving s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹.
One mole of dissolved AgCl supplies one mole of each ion. The square root follows this stoichiometry; it is not a universal rule for all salts.

pages.transition: A one-to-two salt changes both the factor and the power.

pages.title: Worked solubility of a one-to-two salt

blocks.text: Teacher-created rounded data: K(sp)(CaF₂) = 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹. Let molar solubility be s. Then [Ca²⁺] = s and [F⁻] = 2s. K(sp) = s(2s)² = 4s³. Thus s = (4.0 × 10⁻¹¹/4)^(1/3) = 2.15 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. [F⁻] = 4.30 × 10⁻⁴ M.
Solubility and ion concentration are not always equal. A single formula unit can produce multiple ions of one type.

pages.transition: An added common ion changes the saturated composition.

pages.title: A common ion lowers solubility

blocks.text: Adding chloride to AgCl equilibrium increases the dissolution product ratio, favouring return of ions to the solid. At fixed temperature K(sp) stays constant, but equilibrium silver concentration becomes smaller.

Teacher-created example: K(sp) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and added chloride is 0.010 M. If s ≪ 0.010, s(0.010 + s) ≈ 0.010s. Hence s ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ M, much smaller than in pure water. The result checks the approximation.

pages.transition: The same product ratio predicts whether a mixed solution precipitates.

pages.title: Compare ionic product with K(sp)

blocks.text: Q(sp) uses current ion concentrations in the same expression as K(sp). If Q(sp) > K(sp), precipitation is favoured. If Q(sp) < K(sp), the solution is unsaturated and further solid can dissolve if present. Equality describes saturation.

A solution with no visible solid may still be supersaturated temporarily because forming a crystal can be slow. The criterion predicts thermodynamic tendency rather than the exact time precipitation becomes visible.

pages.transition: Mixing dilutes each ion before the precipitation test.

pages.title: Worked precipitation after mixing

blocks.text: Teacher-created example: mix 50.0 mL of 0.010 M AgNO₃ and 50.0 mL of 0.010 M NaCl. Before precipitation, total volume is 100.0 mL. [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = 0.010 × 50.0/100.0 = 0.0050 M. Q(sp) = (0.0050)² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵. This greatly exceeds K(sp) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so AgCl precipitates.

The quotient is evaluated immediately after mixing and before reaction adjustment. Using the original stock concentrations would ignore the dilution, even though precipitation is still predicted in this example.

pages.transition: A second reaction that removes an ion can instead increase dissolution.

pages.title: Acid can increase some salts’ solubility

blocks.text: For a carbonate solid, dissolved CO₃²⁻ can accept H⁺ to become HCO₃⁻ and then carbonic-acid-derived species. Removing free carbonate lowers the dissolution quotient, encouraging more solid to dissolve.

Acid does not universally increase every salt’s solubility. The effect depends on whether the relevant anion is protonated appreciably and on any other equilibria. Chloride, the conjugate base of a strong acid, is not appreciably removed by ordinary protonation in water.

pages.transition: Use these examples to connect the chapter’s equilibrium tools.

pages.title: One quotient idea links the chapter

blocks.text: Molecular equilibrium, acid ionisation, salt hydrolysis and precipitation all compare a current ratio with a temperature-dependent constant. A disturbance changes the composition; the system responds until the appropriate equilibria and charge balance are satisfied.

Acids donate protons, Lewis bases donate electron pairs, buffers consume small additions through conjugate partners, and common ions suppress suitable dissociation equilibria. Each application uses the same equilibrium logic with a different reaction equation.
Comparing raw K(sp) values alone does not always rank solubilities if salts have different dissolution stoichiometries. Convert each to s under the same conditions.

pages.transition: Revise stoichiometry and mixing before solving independently.

pages.title: Revision: small solubility still has exact bookkeeping

blocks.text: Write the dissolution equation, omit the pure solid, and raise each ion concentration to its coefficient. Relate ion concentrations to molar solubility through those same coefficients.

Q(sp) > K(sp) favours precipitation; Q(sp) < K(sp) is unsaturated. Include dilution on mixing and any common ion. pH can alter solubility when it changes free-ion concentration through an additional acid–base equilibrium.

questions.question: For PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻, express K(sp) in terms of pure-water solubility s.
Why is the solid absent from K(sp)?
questions.answer: Its pure-phase activity is constant and incorporated into the equilibrium constant.

questions.question: If Q(sp) is smaller than K(sp), is precipitation favoured?
questions.answer: No. The solution is unsaturated; dissolution is favoured if solid is available.

questions.question: Why calculate concentrations after mixing before testing precipitation?
questions.answer: Each stock solution is diluted by the added volume, and Q(sp) uses the resulting current concentrations.

questions.question: Does a common ion change K(sp) at fixed temperature?
questions.answer: No. It changes the equilibrium composition and often lowers solubility while K(sp) stays fixed.

questions.question: Why can acid dissolve a carbonate more readily?
questions.answer: Protonation removes free carbonate from solution, lowering the dissolution quotient and favouring further dissolution.
